title: Evening reading
hookLine: a few lines of your companion text
tomorrow: Zoe snapped at Dale. say sorry tonight, or sleep on it?

lines: PAGES AN HOUR, BOOKS A YEAR.
cards: Reading apps love to show your pace: pages an hour, books a year, a streak of nights. In the Egyptian desert there was a monk named Pambo with the opposite pace.

He couldn't read, so he went to a teacher to learn a psalm by ear. The teacher began with the first verse: I said, I will take heed to my ways, that I sin not with my tongue. Pambo stopped him right there.
That one is enough for now, he said. And he walked out. He didn't come back for months.
Why would anyone leave a lesson after one line?

teach.b: When the teacher finally found him and scolded him, Pambo said he still hadn't learned the verse. Not memorized it. Learned it.
He meant he was still sinning with his tongue: a sharp word here, a careless one there. Years later a friend asked whether he'd mastered it now, and Pambo said he had barely managed it.
The church historian Socrates Scholasticus tells this story, and it shows what reading meant to the Desert Fathers.

teach.h: READ IN ORDER TO BE DONE.
teach.b: In their tradition, scripture is read in order to be done. Tradition says a monk might carry one verse through the day, saying it over and over while his hands worked, the way you'd keep a smooth stone in your pocket.
Visitors came to the old monks asking, Abba, give me a word: one line to live on, not a library.

That is why monastic reading is slow, a few lines taken in and turned over until they change the way a person talks, and eats, and treats a guest. So the question for tonight isn't how much you read before sleep.
It's whether anything you read comes with you into tomorrow.
Three lines, chosen and carried, can do what forty pages skimmed can't.

how: Christian monks and nuns still read scripture slowly at set times, a practice often called lectio divina; the desert monks carried a single verse through the day's work.

o: a full chapter read fast to finish the book

games.q: your book club wants three chapters a week and you're behind. what would reading Pambo's way look like?
o: take one passage slowly and carry it through your week.
skim all three chapters fast so you can keep up.
drop the club, since reading only counts when you're alone.
games.why: Pambo heard one verse and left to practice it. In the desert tradition, a few lines lived beat many lines covered.

practice: Take the book you keep by your bed, any book that feeds you, and open it anywhere. Read three lines out loud, slowly, then read them once more, a little slower.
Keep the one phrase that catches, and let it ride in and out on your breathing until the bell.

wordCard.voice: Evening reading: a few lines of your companion text before sleep, read slowly enough to carry, the way Pambo carried one verse.

orig.note: Greek, from Aramaic: father. Desert monks called their elders abba.

carryVoice: Keep this one: three lines, carried the way Pambo carried his one verse. See you tomorrow.
